title: Message Passing
body:
One of the two forms of [[Inter-process Communication]]. Processes exchange data by calling
`send` and `receive`, and the [[Kernel|kernel]] carries the message between them. Nothing
is shared: the data is copied out of the sender's address space and into the receiver's.

```
send(destination, message)
receive(source, &message)
```

## Against [[Shared Memory]]

| | [[Message Passing]] | [[Shared Memory]] |
|---|---|---|
| Data lives | in the kernel, copied twice | in one region mapped into both address spaces |
| Speed | slower, two copies and a [[System Call]] per message | fast, plain memory access after setup |
| Synchronization | comes free; the kernel serializes | yours to write, with [[Semaphores]] |
| Works across machines | yes, this is what sockets are | no |

**The trade is speed against difficulty.** Shared memory is fast but you own the
[[Critical Section Problem]] yourself. Message passing has the kernel do the coordination,
so there is no shared state to race on, and you pay for that in copies and system calls.

## Blocking or not

- **Blocking send**: the sender waits until the message is received. Blocking `receive`:
  the receiver waits until one arrives, entering the [[Waiting state]].
- **Non-blocking send**: hand it to the kernel and carry on. Non-blocking `receive`: take a
  message if there is one, otherwise return nothing.

Blocking send with blocking receive is a *rendezvous*: both sides meet at the message, and
neither proceeds without the other. The buffered non-blocking version needs a queue in the
kernel, which is a [[Bounded Buffer Problem]] with the kernel as the shared buffer.
